newsitem.title: BULGARIA: SEVEN YEARS ON, BULGARIA GOVT UNDER PRESSURE AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: SEVEN YEARS ON, BULGARIA GOVT UNDER PRESSURE AGAIN.

text.p: Reformers in Bulgaria's ruling Socialist Party meet on Monday to discuss calls for a cabinet and policy shakeup, seven years after Communist Party reformers forced the resignation of hardline leader Todor Zhivkov.
While no one expects the Socialist government to quit, the parallels between 1989 and 1996 show how little things have progressed in seven years of transition.

Hardliners and reformists are struggling for supremacy in the ruling party, the economy is collapsing, and last week's presidential election showed the hearts of the electorate are with the anti-communist opposition.

"It is obvious that during these seven years, this system has led the country to collapse. Without radical, quick, even drastic change to put a stop to the evils in the banking sector, the economy of the country will continue to decline," Prime Minister Zhan Videnov wrote in the party daily Douma.

The opposition, buoyed by Petar Stoyanov's victory in last Sunday's presidential election run-off, says it will work towards early parliamentary elections to remove the Socialist government, now halfway through its four-year term.
The International Monetary Fund, for its part, is trying to find a formula to shore up the economy and prevent Bulgaria from defaulting on its $10 billion foreign debt.
It has proposed a currency board system which would effectively peg the lev to the dollar or the mark, halting its fall and bringing inflation under control.
On November 10, 1989, the day after the Berlin Wall came down, Bulgarian Communist Party reformers forced out Zhivkov in a palace coup.

Today, while Bulgaria's former Warsaw Pact allies press for membership of NATO and the European Union, the small Balkan state still looks more to Moscow than to Brussels and has the lowest level of foreign investment in the region.
"No one is suggesting things are as bad as they were in 1989, but in economic reform terms, even countries like Albania and Romania are doing better," one diplomat said.

The chairman of the Socialists' reformist Union for Social Democracy (USD) wing, Chavdar Kyuranov, told Reuters the different economic programmes followed by six successive governments since 1989 had created the current disorder.
He singled out the Videnov government's heavy taxes on small and medium businesses. "We needed to strengthen the state, but this is too much. Entrepreneurship is being stifled," he said.
A criticism often levelled against Videnov is that his commitment to private enterprise is limited to the business associates making up his so-called "friendly circle".

Nineteen leading Socialists, including party vice-chairman Yanaki Stoilov, signed a letter in Douma on Tuesday calling for a new cabinet containing economic experts with practical experience, and concrete plans to avert food shortages and stabilise the crumbling banking system.

"The question is not whether there should be reform, but how it should be implemented," said Kyuranov. He said he hoped the reformists could work from within to alter party policy and avert a split into hardline and reformist camps.
Foreign Minister Georgi Pirinski is a prominent reformist, as was former prime minister Andrei Lukanov, gunned down outside his home on October 2 in an apparent contract killing.

Pressure has mounted on Videnov over the past week and newspapers have been full of calls for his resignation, but the premier said on Saturday he hoped the Socialists could resolve their problems internally.
"I will definitely not seek a confidence vote in parliament, I will seek a confidence vote from Socialist deputies and party leaders on Monday," Videnov told reporters.
